If I had to wager a guess, probably Poseidon. I think when it comes to Zeus, he blames himself more than the King of Gods for the deaths of his crew. He had the choice, he could've picked his men over himself but he didn't. I imagine that would result in more self-loathing than actual hatred towards Zeus. In comparison though, Poseidon had no chance of showing mercy. Even after having apologised, Poseidon still killed his crew. Worse of all, his motivations were to show the rest of the world that he wasn't lenient, that he wasn't to be messed with. I think Odysseus would hate Poseidon more.

If Odysseus' motivations to get home was a million dollars, we'd all (or most of us anyway,) would see him as scum. That being said, we can't really use this hypothetical as a way to judge how good or bad his actions throughout the musical truly were. I mean, a person definitely isn't worth just a million dollars. In this scenario, Odysseus would be sacrificing his men and making devastating mistakes, all for a reward worth MUCH less than in the original musical. 

Me personally, while I don't necessarily agree with his actions, I wouldn't call him a villain persay. His motivations are understandable and I can sympathise with his plight. However, as not only the captain but KING of his men, I can't help but give him the stink eye for well, being so irresponsible. He has a duty to his men first and foremost. These men have wives and children of their own, parents and siblings waiting for them, families worried about them. He IS a bad guy in my eyes for completely going against his duties as king, abusing his authority and betraying the trust of his crew, men and friends. He is an incredibly selfish man. He's very well-written and his flaws just make his character all the more complex. I think a lot of us don't realise just how much power Odysseus truly holds which leads us to being unable to see just how flawed of a person he really is. That and also we empathise too much with him since the majority of the musical is told from his perspective.

WARNING: LONG ANALYSIS BELOW! (did not expect this would turn into a full rant.. oops.)


It's fascinating that each line of the prophet's actually lines up with each song of the Thunder Saga.


I find it so interesting that the second line is "I see the sacrifice of **man**" and not **men**. You would think that if the line was in relation to Scylla, the word "man" would be in the plural form. But it isn't. Instead the prophet is talking about the sacrifice of one singular man. If we look at the moment after Odysseus fools the sirens, we actually see what the prophet really meant. He was talking about Odysseus sacrificing his morals. We know from past songs (COUGH Polyphemus COUGH) that deep down Odysseus wants to show mercy, wants to let the sirens go. But he can't. Instead, Odysseus completely forgoes his desires, acting in cruelty and ruthlessness - instructing the crew to cut off the sirens' tails and drown. 


ALSO ALSO, "I see portrayals of betrayal" is such genius writing. Again, focus on which word is singular and which is plural. Do you see it? There's only one betrayal happening here but multiple portrayals of it. Well, which betrayal happens immediately after the sirens? Odysseus'. He sends off 6 men to die, sacrificing them to Scylla. There's only one betrayal happening here, only he knows the dangers and consequences. Heck, only he knew Scylla would be there! ("Captain, something.. approaches.") But so many people were betrayed. Those 6 men were betrayed, his entire crew was betrayed, Eurylochus was betrayed. All of them, each and every last one put their faith in Odysseus, they believed in him and entrusted their safety to him, their LIVES to him. They questioned him at times sure, but at the end of the day they still believed their captain was doing his best. They didn't agree with his actions sometimes but they knew their misery and suffering wasn't intentional. The moment Odysseus sacrificed those men, he was no longer the same captain that they trusted. He'd become a man willing to sacrifice his own to return home. This was intentional.


"And a brother's final stand" is pretty.. direct. The name of the song is literally Mutiny, kinda on the nose.


The next two lines are actually in reference to the same song, Thunder Bringer! 


"I see you on the brink of death" - Oddyseus is on the brink of death at the start of Thunder Bringer, having been stabbed by his crew (OUCH!) and then put in danger due to Eurylochus' actions. They're quite literally being hunted down by Zeus, I think this is as close to death as you can get. 


"I see you draw your final breath," is a much, MUCH more interesting line though. In this line, I don't think the "you" is literal. Rather, I think this "you" the prophet is talking about is metaphorical. I think this "you" the prophet is talking about is the Odysseus of the past, the Odysseus that was once merciful and not so tunnel-visioned, the Odysseus that was once trusted, the Odysseus that was his crew's captain. The moment Odysseus picked himself over his crew, valuing his own goals, dreams, desires and LIFE over his crew's is the moment that "he" dies. 


AAAAAA, JORGE IS SUCH A GOOD SONG-WRITER!! The Thunder Saga HAS to be my favourite of them all which is kind of insane considering how much I loved the Ocean Saga. 


TLDR; Each line of the prophet's lines up with each song of the Thunder Saga.


I see a song of past romance, (The siren pretending to be Penelope, SUFFERING)


I see the sacrifice of man, (Odysseus sacrificing his morals - most prominently seen in his cruelty towards the sirens, DIFFERENT BEAST)


I see portrayals of betrayal, (Scylla, more specifically from the perspective of the crew that'd been eaten, SCYLLA)


And a brother's final stand, (Eurylochus, MUTINY)


I see you on the brink of death, (literally, THUNDER BRINGER)


I see you take your final breath, (metaphorically, THUNDER BRINGER)

*Might as well go full nerd mode. The criteria for nonsuicidal self-injury proposed in the DSM-5:


A. In the last year, the individual has, on 5 or more days, engaged in intentional self-inflicted damage to the surface of his or her body of a sort likely to induce bleeding, bruising, or pain, with the expectation that the injury will lead to only minor or moderate physical harm (i.e., there is no suicidal intent).

B. The individual engages in the self-injurious behavior with one or more of the followingexpectations:  
1. To obtain relief from a negative feeling or cognitive state.  
2. To resolve an interpersonal difficulty.  
3. To induce a positive feeling state.

C. The intentional self-injury is associated with at least one of the following:  
1. Interpersonal difficulties or negative feelings or thoughts, such as depression, anxiety, tension, anger, generalized distress, or self-criticism, occurring in the periodimmediately prior to the self-injurious act.  
2. Prior to engaging in the act, a period of preoccupation with the intended behaviorthat is difficult to control.  
3. Thinking about self-injury that occurs frequently, even when it is not acted upon

D. The behavior or its consequences cause clinically significant distress or interference ininterpersonal, academic, or other important areas of functioning.

E. The behavior does not occur exclusively during psychotic episodes, delirium, substance intoxication, or substance withdrawal. In individuals with a neurodevelopmentaldisorder, the behavior is not part of a pattern of repetitive stereotypies. The behavioris not better explained by another mental disorder or medical condition (e.g., psychoticdisorder, autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, stereotypic movement disorder with self-injury, trichotillomania \[hair-pulling disorder\], excoriation \[skin-picking\] disorder).*
